submission.natural_language_explanation: This pole fires when a passage is naming specific places: it peaks on the comma, 'and', 'of', 'in' or 'for' that introduces or joins place names in a list or relation ('Nelson, Marlborough, Canterbury, Otago and Southland'; 'the island of Java'; 'canton of Valais'; 'the street in Chiba'; 'Dirksen of Illinois') and on the first subword of such a name (' Ot' of Otago, ' South' of Southland, ' Ever' of Everett). It stays near zero when the identical slot is filled by ordinary nouns ('villages, districts, counties, regions and provinces'), by a generic locative ('the island', 'the region', 'the capital', 'a small city'), or by a single major city name (Chicago, Dallas, London, Paris).

The county council commissioned an independent review after the spring floods damaged bridges and culverts across the upper catchment. The review panel met for eleven weeks, heard from more than forty witnesses, and read submissions from farmers, anglers, hauliers and residents' associations. Its chairman, a retired engineer named Margaret Ellison, had spent thirty years working on drainage schemes in the lowlands and was known for insisting on measured language and verifiable figures. The panel's remit was narrow: to establish how much water the system could carry under present conditions, how the maintenance budget had been spent over the previous decade, and whether the forecast used by planners still reflected the rainfall records.

The evidence painted a familiar picture. Spending on routine dredging had fallen steadily since the regional authority was reorganised, while the number of blocked culverts reported by parish councils had more than doubled. Several witnesses described the same sequence of events: a summer of maintenance deferred, an autumn of heavy rain, a winter of flooded kitchens and closed roads. The panel noted that the authority's own inspectors had flagged sixteen sites as high risk in a report three years earlier, and that only four of those sites had since been visited. Nobody could say where the remaining money had gone.

A second theme concerned communication. Residents said they had learned of the flood warning only when water reached their front doors, even though the monitoring station upstream had recorded a sharp rise the previous evening. The authority accepted that its alerting system had failed but argued that the failure was technical rather than institutional. The panel was not persuaded. It observed that a system designed without consultation is likely to fail without anyone noticing, and recommended that the alerting service be tested publicly twice a year.

The panel also examined the condition of the older structures. Many of the bridges were built in the nineteenth century and were never designed for the weight of modern agricultural machinery. At one crossing, the parapet had been rebuilt twice in fifteen years. At another, the deck had dropped by almost a hand's breadth, a movement that had gone unrecorded because no survey had been carried out since the closure of the district office. The panel recommended a programme of structural surveys, phased over five years and funded from the capital budget rather than the maintenance budget.

Finally, the panel considered what should happen next. It rejected the idea of a single large engineering scheme, arguing that the cost could not be justified and that the benefits would be concentrated downstream. Instead it favoured a series of small interventions, each designed with the parish involved and each monitored for at least three years. It also asked the authority to publish its maintenance schedule in full, so that residents could see what was planned and what had been delayed. Engineers inspected the weirs at Kelso, Jedburgh, Hawick, Selkirk and Galashiels before the report was published, and their notes were appended as an annex. The council accepted most of the recommendations and promised a further report in the autumn.
